steps.title: Two phases, two clusters
steps.bodyHtml: Serving an LLM has two very different halves. Prefill reads the whole prompt in one dense, compute-hungry pass. Decode then generates one token at a time, limited by memory bandwidth rather than raw compute. Because their hardware appetites differ, modern serving stacks disaggregate them: the left pool only runs prefills, the right pool only decodes. The bridge between them carries exactly one thing — the KV cache — and we'll follow it shortly. Each of the {nodesTotal} nodes here is one serving instance: 8 GPUs, 2 pipeline stages, 4-way tensor parallelism.

steps.title: Inside one instance: TP and PP
steps.bodyHtml: Watch this single prefill instance. Each row of 4 GPUs is a tensor-parallel group: every layer of the model ends with an all-reduce across the row — the cyan shimmer on the thick NVLink rails. This is the busiest traffic in the whole building, yet it never leaves the node: NVLink traffic is invisible to the datacenter fabric. The two rows are pipeline stages; the model's layers are split between them, and activations hop from stage 0 to stage 1 as white pulses on the diagonal link.

steps.title: Follow one request end-to-end
steps.bodyHtml: Everything else is frozen; one request plays on a loop. A user's prompt hits the router, which tokenizes it and picks a prefill instance. The prefill burst lights up: hot TP shimmer, activation hops, and — already — KV pages streaming out to the decode instance. When prefill finishes, decode takes over: a slower, dimmer, steady rhythm, with a thin green trickle of generated tokens looping back to the router and out to the user. One request, one direction, no coordination with anything else.

steps.title: The KV-cache transfer
steps.bodyHtml: The only reason these two pools talk at all: prefill produces the KV cache — the model's working memory of the prompt — and decode needs it. Watch the amber stream on the inter-pool links. Two things matter. It is one-way: KV flows prefill→decode, never back. And it is layerwise-overlapped: transfer begins while prefill is still running, layer by layer, so the smear tracks prefill progress instead of arriving as one lump at the end. Each request produces one such burst, then that link goes quiet.

steps.title: The storage tier: prefix reuse
steps.bodyHtml: Prompts repeat — system prompts, long documents, multi-turn chats. So finished KV caches don't always die. Watch two scripted requests: the first is a cache hit — its prefix KV is fetched from storage up into the prefill pool, and the prefill burst that follows is visibly shorter. The second request completes and flushes its KV down to storage for later reuse. The storage tier is bidirectional, but every flow is triggered by an individual request's lifecycle — there is no schedule, no clock, no sweep.

steps.title: Zoom out: no heartbeat
steps.bodyHtml: Traffic is back on. Let it run and squint. Requests arrive at random — a Poisson process — and each one marches through its own private lifecycle, indifferent to every other. Pools are busy asynchronously; there is never a moment when all links flash together. Now look at the rhythm strip below: aggregate fabric traffic is ragged, structureless noise. An outside observer measuring this cable plant would see hum, not pulse. Hold that image — then switch to Training mode and run its tour. Also see what this animation lies about.
